headlines.summary: Intel’s turnaround now hinges on proving its foundry strategy can deliver, as customers look for signs the company will add fab capacity and catch TSMC
headlines.article_text: Intel foundry faces critical test after stock's 45% plunge in October Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel's 29% drop on Friday left the stock down 45% in October, its worst month on record, according to FactSet. Intel sees the global market for server CPUs growing fivefold to $200 billion in the next five years, but the softening PC market is hurting legacy revenue. Intel is redirecting some 18A capacity in Oregon fabs to make Intel 3 chips for its server CPUs In this article INTC TSM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive officer of Intel Corp., attends the company's event in Tokyo, Japan, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Akio Kon | Bloomberg | Getty Images As Intel comes off its steepest stock drop since the 1970s due to a worsening outlook for the PC market, the chipmaker is facing intensifying pressure to get its flailing foundry business off the ground. It's been an elusive task for Intel. The company has spent half a decade, and a good chunk of its $108 billion in capital expenditures over that stretch, trying to challenge Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company . But it still has no marquee customer for its most advanced chips, and is primarily manufacturing chips for its own products. Wall Street is losing patience. After the U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, the stock started to shoot up, ultimately rising sixfold over 10 months before peaking in June. Intel was finally finding its niche in the artificial intelligence boom, delivering central processors used for agentic AI, while optimism simultaneously grew over its fab aspirations. Intel's story took a dramatic turn for the worse on Thursday, when the company said revenue this quarter will be between $1 billion and $2 billion shy of analysts' estimates as the PC market continues to suffer from soaring costs for memory and other components. Intel still counts on its PC segment for roughly half of its revenue, and consumers are increasingly choosing not to upgrade. The stock plummeted 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, capping off a 45% plunge in October, the steepest monthly drop on record, according to FactSet. It's down another 8% in Monday trading. Intel vs. Nasdaq since start of October Intel's investments in the future are supposed to be paying off. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion. Intel's data center business recorded 78% growth in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.3 billion. However, Intel said it can't make enough chips to fill demand, pointing to industry-wide supply constraints for wafers, substrates and memory, many of the same factors hurting PC sales. That's forcing Tan to make some hard choices. In response to the capacity shortage, Intel said it's shifting some Oregon factory capacity away from making wafers for its advanced 18A chips to make more wafers on an older node, known as Intel 3, which are used for its data center products. Intel is counting on 18A to attract outside foundry customers, so the shift in resources could complicate that effort. David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who previously spent almost three decades on Intel's board, said the latest moves are hardly welcoming to prospective foundry customers. "They're concerned that if Intel doesn't actually have excess capacity beyond its own demand, that they're just not a very credible supplier," Yoffie said. If it doesn't find a large-scale foundry customer within a year, "then the stress on Intel's economics are going to start to show even more dramatically," he said. Intel didn't respond to a request for comment. Intel is best known for its industry-leading central processing units, or CPUs. Graphics processing units from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices ruled the early AI boom because they excel at handling large workloads for training models and inference for chatbots, while CPUs like Intel's are crucial for running the virtual machines used by agentic apps like Meta 's Muse. Competitor or partner? As one of the only companies in the world capable of manufacturing and packaging the advanced chips it needs for its own products, Intel has "more control over their destiny" than most chipmakers, Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview. "If you don't have enough capacity, you leave revenue and money on the table," Klein said. Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, who was ousted in late 2024, spent his four-year tenure at the company aggressively pursuing foundry investments to catch up after delays on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies, advanced process nodes that aim to fit more transistors on each chip. Tan has taken a more cautious approach, limiting spending until customer demand is locked in. He said on Thursday that "a couple customers" would be announced in the coming two quarters. watch now VIDEO 16:50 16:50 Can Intel’s New Arizona Chip Fab Bring It Back From The Brink? Tech Intel's 18A chips, for its own use, are in high-volume production out of Arizona, with a second fab in the works. A first structural truss was just installed at Intel's new Ohio facility, although the project is nearly five years behind schedule . Another roadblock to getting new customers, Yoffie said, is that chipmakers like Broadcom and Qualcomm may hesitate to manufacture chips at a company that's also a competitor on the product side. "The right solution is for Intel to spin off the foundry business," Yoffie said, calling it "not only the best solution, but maybe the only solution." Klein said AMD is likely the only major chipmaker that isn't interested in manufacturing at Intel because the two companies compete directly in the CPU market. He called it a "competitive, secrecy, privacy issue." AMD reports third-quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. Yoffie said the U.S. needs Intel to succeed. "Ultimately, TSMC can only create maybe 20-25% of their global capacity in the United States and that will still take several years," he said. "If we have no American foundry and we run into any number of geopolitical problems, supply chain problems like we had under Covid, that is going to be bad for the country and bad for the American semiconductor industry." headlines.article_text: Stock market today: Live updates Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Oct. 30, 2026. Brendan McDermid | Reuters The Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 fell on Monday, giving up earlier gains, as investors continued to move out of tech stocks and add exposure to other parts of the market. The tech-heavy Nasdaq dipped 0.6%, while the S&P 500 shed 0.2%. Both benchmarks were up as much as 1.4% and 1.1%, respectively. The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 328 points, or 0.6%. Shares of Nvidia and Meta Platforms dipped 0.5% and 0.7%, respectively. Apple, which reports earnings after the bell, traded 2% lower. Marvell Technology shares dropped about 12%, while Lumentum shed 18% after the companies announced that Marvell is buying Lumentum in a $115 billion deal . Oracle shares also declined 8% after the company said it plans to sell $10 billion in common stock as well as $10 billion in bonds to finance its AI buildout. Gains in so-called old economy stocks such as Sherwin-Williams and Home Deport powered the Dow, rising 5.6% and 3.3%, respectively. Honeywell International, 3M and Boeing were also up more than 2% each. Nasdaq intraday chart The rotation out of tech after the major U.S. stock benchmarks suffered a losing week, as investors continued to scrutinize names related to the AI buildout. "The stock market's longer-term bullish narrative may have taken some hits in recent weeks, but it's still intact," said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E-Trade. "The challenge has been short-term momentum — stringing together more than a few days without being disrupted by surging oil prices, concerns about AI spending, inflation, or geopolitics." Last week, the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the S&P 500 logged a losing October amid AI spending concerns, with the Nasdaq suffering its worst losses since March 2025. The Dow, however, rose almost 2% as investors rotated into defensive areas like healthcare. "The market has more potential 'volatility triggers' to face — including this week's midterms and jobs data — but its ability to bend but not break under pressure has been a positive sign," Larkin added. The U.S. midterm elections will be held on Tuesday, when Democrats are expected to take control of the House of Representatives, while Senate control remains uncertain. Meanwhile, Brent crude tumbled nearly 8% to around $104 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures also pulled back more than 7% to roughly $96. Oil prices fell amid hopes that the U.S. and Iran may resume peace talks, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying over the weekend that President Donald Trump "hasn't made a decision" to attack Iran and that Washington would prefer to resolve the conflict "peacefully." Iranian state media also reported that the country's foreign minister said an agreement with is possible if the U.S. "demonstrates goodwill." Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated the move in oil prices in the session. 29 Min Ago Stephens upgrades Oracle to overweight A sign is posted in front of an Oracle campus on September 10, 2025 in Redwood Shores, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Stephens upgraded Oracle to overweight from equal weight on Monday. "We believe the market needs to give Oracle more credit for the execution on delivering compute that continues to happen," wrote Analyst Brett Huff, who noted the company delivered about 850 MW in the first quarter across 38 projects in 11 countries. Huff added it sees Oracle may reach "double-digit" multi-year growth in applications, higher than what Wall Street's 10% growth estimate. The firm gave Oracle a $213 price target, implying a roughly 63% upside from Friday's close. — Ananya Chetia 1 Hour Ago Stocks making big moves: Oracle, IDEXX Laboratories, Tempus AI Check out some of the companies making the biggest moves midday: Oracle — The database software giant slumped another 6% after filing plans Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence build-out. Oracle will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. IDEXX Laboratories — Shares climbed 20% after the veterinary diagnostics company topped third-quarter earnings and revenue estimates, driven by growth in its Companion Animal Group. IDEXX posted third-quarter revenue of $1.21 billion, 10% above the year-earlier period. IDEXX also raised its 2026 revenue and earnings forecasts while lowering its operating-margin outlook. Tempus AI — The precision-medicine company rose nearly 12% after third-quarter earnings, revenue and adjusted EBITDA beat Wall Street estimates. Revenue climbed 23% to $411.5 million, with data and applications growing 33% and oncology volume growth accelerating to 32%. Tempus also raised its 2026 revenue forecast and reiterated the adjusted EBITDA outlook. The investment bank has a price target of $100 on the stock. The downgrade is due to pressures on referral traffic as AI supplants traditional internet searching at the dominant search engine Google . The bank also has concerns about mandatory log-ins for the site, monetization trends, and the prospects for Google's licensing deal with Reddit. "It seems increasingly likely that Google does not renew its licensing agreement expiring early 2027," Rob Sanderson at Loop Capital wrote. Google reported a significant dent in its core advertising revenues last week, leading to its largest single-day stock decline ever on Thursday. — Tobias Burns 3 Hours Ago Construction spending hits lowest since April 2020 Workers put up wood framing for a home under construction at the Lilac Ridge community by Lennar Homes in Vacaville, California, July 14, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Construction spending in September fell at its fastest monthly level since the Covid pandemic, weighed by a sharp drop in residential activity. The Commerce Department reported Monday that the metric slipped 1.9% for the month, posting the biggest monthly decline since April 2020. On a year-over-year basis, construction spending was off 2.7%. Residential spending was off 5.5%, more than offsetting a 0.6% increase in nonresidential outlays. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for an increase of 0.4%. Private construction spending fell 2.4%, while public construction expenditures were off 0.1%. — Jeff Cox 4 Hours Ago Deutsche Bank goes bullish on tech Deutsche Bank has shifted back to an overweight rating on the tech sector after downgrading it to neutral earlier this month amid ongoing volatility. The sector's "relative performance is now at the bottom of its long-run trend channel, a level from which it has V-turned up 5 times in the last 2 1/2 years," analyst Parag Thatte said in a Friday note to clients. The Nasdaq-100 slid roughly 8% since Deutsche Bank issued its downgrade to a neutral rating on Oct. 9. On Friday alone, the index dropped by about 3.5%. Now, analysts at the bank see the trend reversing, with potentially positive effects for the broader market. "The risk-reward now favors going overweight again. "Robert and I are thrilled that our gift of over 2 million shares of SpaceX stock will be distributed to children's Trump accounts in December!" President and COO Gwynne Shotwell wrote in the post. The gift from Shotwell and her husband will provide a share apiece to around 2 million Trump Accounts holders ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less, or in ZIP codes with too few residents for a median family income to be reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 8% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank 13%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." headlines.summary: Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new shares and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
headlines.article_text: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds, it said in a filing. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. In this article ORCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled more than 6% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. Oracle's one-day performance The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.267%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 296, up 270% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026 While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out." — CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.
